awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Multi-sited Geophysical Archaeology for the Study of Rural Settlement Change and Continuity
awd_abstract_narration:
Across global contexts, buried settlements are rich resources, preserving the daily lives and practices of their occupants. However, in the complexity and, frequently, large spatial scale of such sites, they present a host of challenges for the researcher. This is especially true for sites that leave little trace above ground, the study of which would typically require intensive and expansive excavation to recover meaningful datasets. This dissertation project has developed an alternative methodology for the study of settlements tested across a multi-sited landscape. The method combines geophysical techniques capable of non-destructively visualizing buried sites and targeted soil coring based upon geophysical datasets to recover subsurface samples for later laboratory analysis. This workflow addresses traditional limitations in the study of buried landscapes, allowing for spatial breadth but also the recovery of stratified subsurface data at significant depths, with special pertinence for fieldwork under time and/or budgetary constraints. The project provides educational and training opportunities for students.

The research compares the morphology and chronology of dispersed settlements and nucleated villages. Relationships between the construction, modification, and abandonment of dispersed and nucleated settlements provides insight into cultural practices, with methodological contributions to settlement and landscape study.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This grant funded a dissertation that reopens the chronology of the Irish ringfort. Roughly 45,000 of these earthen and stone enclosures survive across the island, which are conventionally dated to a window in the Early Middle Ages (600-1000 AD) and are broadly understood as the quintessential dispersed agricultural settlement of that era. However, the tight association between the site type and the time period has been shaped as much by the historical context of archaeology in Ireland as by actual material evidence. To test ringfort chronology, this project developed and applied a methodology called para-excavation, which combines field survey, magnetometry, ground-penetrating radar, and targeted soil coring to recover stratigraphically controlled radiocarbon samples from many sites in a single region without full excavation. 

Through the Geophysical Ringfort Archaeological Survey Project (GRASP), para-excavation was applied to nine ringforts in and around the civil parish of Ballintober, Co. Roscommon, between 2023 and 2025. The study yielded 47 radiocarbon dates from eight sites, centering on a time span from the early fourth century BC to the late seventeenth century AD. The results confirm an early medieval floruit, but place the regional peak at 800-850 AD, roughly 150 years later than the island-wide peak. Four sites produced Iron Age dates, including five determinations from stratified contexts at Rath Maol (site number RO034-006). A regional gap in activity from approximately 50-250 AD aligns with the "Late Iron Age Lull' observed widely across Ireland. At the other end, four sites yielded post-1000 AD activity, much of it from the types of shallow or disturbed contexts most vulnerable to taphonomic destruction and analytical exclusion; the seeming sharpness of ringfort decline after the turn of the millennium might be partly an artifact of site formation processes in the past or sampling strategies in the present. 

Taken together, the GRASP sites demonstrate consistent human engagement with the same locations across more than two millennia, spanning periods that conventional chronology treats as fundamentally separate. Periodization is a necessary tool for archaeology, but recent advances in absolute dating now make it possible to build chronologies from the ground up, site by site and region by region, rather than fitting new evidence into inherited frameworks. Like many other Irish site types, ringforts are best understood as persistent places: locations whose stories extend far beyond the construction of the standing monument, and which reward close regional study, attentive to the full range and complexity of their evidence. 

On a personal note, I am very grateful to the federal government for its support of this research; without the NSF, the work would have been impossible. Specifically, I would like to thank Dr. John Yellen, Project Director of the NSF. This grant is one of the last-awarded dissertation improvement grants for Archaeology; the funding stream has dried up. I hope that it returns; both the funding itself, and the peer-review process, were integral to the success of the dissertation.
